folios.label: Capability / invention
folios.question: Can AI do whole tasks, and reliably?

rows.line: The length of task AI can finish keeps doubling about every four months.
rows.who: AI Futures Project (Kokotajlo, Lifland, Jurkovic et al.)

rows.line: Models still cannot learn on the job the way people do, and it holds them back.
Each test AI passes shows the test's limits, not that AI has arrived.
Data-centre buildings and their power hookups are the bottleneck.
If the trend speeds up, by March 2027 AI could reliably do software tasks that take people years.
rows.who: AI Futures Project (Kokotajlo, Lifland, Jurkovic et al.)

rows.line: Models might do most of a software engineer's work end to end within six to twelve months.
Whole projects stay far behind single skills, with the best score on real freelance projects below [test:frontier_uneven].
rows.settles: The best model completing most of the Remote Labor Index's projects.

rows.line: The length of the software tasks AI can finish keeps doubling at least as fast as the scenario assumes, every [test:horizon_fast] or less.
rows.settles: The doubling time lengthening beyond what the scenario assumes.

rows.line: The agents Princeton's tracker tests grow more dependable far more slowly than they grow more accurate.
rows.settles: Reliability rising as fast as accuracy across the next models the tracker tests.

rows.line: AI speeds up its own invention
rows.settles: AI starts speeding up its own invention if independent tests show agents doing more than a day of research work for each day a person puts in, and needing a person's help on long tasks less than half the time.

rows.line: An AI that codes better than the best people arrives in 2027.
If scaling continues, AI as able as a country of geniuses arrives within a year or two.
AI improving itself cannot get past limits that sit outside the lab.
OpenAI builds an automated AI researcher by March 2028.
OpenAI has an automated AI research intern by September 2026.
Memory and chip packaging are short.
Labs and companies keep paying more for the steps models cannot yet take, even as each new model takes more of them on its own.
rows.settles: What labs and companies pay for practice work and for fitting models falling as the models improve.

rows.line: Better data, more than better model designs, drives how much a model learns from its training, so progress comes to rest on finding new data.
rows.settles: Design changes, not data, turning out to carry the gains at the largest scale.

rows.line: Research speeds up far more in software and mathematics than in drug development, materials or physics, where the slowest steps are experiments.
rows.settles: A broad speed-up in the experiment-heavy sciences at the same time as in software.

rows.line: AI's help with AI research brings steady gains, not accelerating ones.
rows.settles: Each new model's gains on AI research tasks coming faster than the last's, with nothing lost along the way.

rows.line: As the scenario is written, AI completes most real, paid freelance projects end to end by the end of 2027.

folios.label: Innovation: products and applications
folios.question: What gets built on it, and who sells it?

rows.line: Practice tasks with automatic graders, and the expert-written data they consume, are where the shortage goes next.
Checking AI's work is sold as a category of its own.
rows.settles: No independent category forming, the checks staying inside the labs' and clouds' own platforms.
rows.who: This site, extending Gillian Hadfield and Andrew Koh

rows.line: Insurers write AI's mistakes out of their standard policies, so the cover has to be bought and priced on its own.
rows.settles: Standard policies going on covering AI's mistakes at no extra price.
rows.who: This site, extending Gillian Hadfield and Andrew Koh

rows.line: Proof of what an AI agent (a model that carries out tasks with software tools on a person's behalf) did, and who answers for it, becomes a bottleneck once agents handle money.
Large platforms move to keep outside agents off them more often than they let them in.
rows.settles: Platforms opening to outside agents more often than they block them, counted under one rule for both; this site's hand-kept ledger does not yet sweep both sides that way, so it tests nothing yet.
rows.who: Byrne Hobart and Nikhil Davar and Soren Larson

rows.line: Labs spend more each year with the firms that sell practice tasks, graders and expert data.
rows.settles: That spending falling once each firm counted a year ago has reported again; the hand-kept tally of disclosed deals is too thin to test it yet.

rows.line: Insurers sell cover written for AI's mistakes, not only exclusions from standard policies.
rows.settles: AI cover staying a niche product that large buyers do not purchase.

rows.line: If training a model further on a firm's own work keeps getting cheaper, apps train their own instead of renting the best.
rows.settles: Apps built on open models still paying labs' prices because training their own stays too costly.

rows.line: The first large failure of a market run by AI agents comes from no one being able to check what an agent did, not from agents lacking skill.
rows.settles: The first large agent failure traced to agents that could not do the work.
rows.who: This site, extending Gillian Hadfield and Andrew Koh

folios.label: Diffusion: early adoption
folios.question: How fast do firms and people take it up?

rows.line: AI's big economic effects arrive over decades, not years.
Adoption stays slow wherever mistakes are costly.
In the jobs most exposed to AI, workers in their early twenties fall behind workers over fifty [cite:canaries], while in the least exposed jobs they do not.
rows.settles: The same gap opening in the least exposed jobs.

rows.line: AI is not an ordinary technology
rows.settles: AI stops looking like an ordinary technology if three things happen together. Models become nearly as reliable on long jobs as on short ones, and not just because the tests have run out of longer tasks. Most of the labour-market trackers we follow break at the same time. And either the share of work hours done with AI passes a fifth, or productivity runs well above trend for years on end.

rows.line: The share of American firms using AI stays within the pace this site calls normal, below [test:firms_normal].
rows.settles: The share of firms using AI climbing past that pace.

rows.line: No single leap in ability unlocks AI's economic value.
Agents take hold first in job search, property and other matching markets.
rows.settles: Agents spreading first in markets where people rarely hire human agents.

rows.line: AI does not wipe out software engineering jobs, and demand for engineers may rise as software gets cheaper to make.
rows.settles: Software engineering employment falling as AI coding tools spread.

rows.line: Official output statistics miss most of AI's gains, which come as better quality and saved time that no price records.
rows.settles: Official statistics capturing AI's gains in quality and saved time as use spreads.
rows.who: Diane Coyle and John Lourenze Poquiz

folios.label: Diffusion: adaptation
folios.question: What happens to work, pay and output as firms reorganise?

rows.line: Workers stop sharing the gains
rows.settles: The case that workers share in AI's gains fails if the typical full-time worker's pay, after inflation, sits below its level at the end of 2022, just before ChatGPT, for four quarters running while the economy's output keeps growing. Pascual Restrepo, an economist who models work once machines can do every task, finds that workers' total pay never falls below its level before such AI unless something else, such as market power over computing, gets in the way; the typical worker's pay is the nearest measure this site reads.

rows.line: In no quarter before 2034 does American real output per person stand [test:no_growth_jump] or more above the highest level it had reached a year or more before.
rows.settles: A quarter before 2034 that clears the bet's line.
rows.who: Benjamin Moll, Alex Imas and five others

rows.line: The economists' scenarios only pull apart after 2027.
rows.who: Korinek et al. (The Anthropic Institute, WP 2026-02)

rows.line: Extreme case: growth soars and workers' share of income falls sharply.
rows.who: Korinek et al. (The Anthropic Institute, WP 2026-02)

rows.line: Modest case: AI adds under half a point a year to growth by 2030.
rows.who: Korinek, Jones, Sacher, Cotter and McCrory (The Anthropic Institute, WP 2026-02)

rows.line: Substantial case: output rises and some office jobs go by 2030.
rows.who: Korinek et al. (The Anthropic Institute, WP 2026-02)

rows.line: As AI takes over paid work, governments move tax from wages towards spending, and later towards AI itself.
rows.settles: Tax systems unchanged as AI does a growing share of the work.
rows.who: This site, extending Anton Korinek and Lee M. Lockwood

rows.line: In some quarter before 2034, output per person stands [test:bet_fast_side] or more above the highest level it had reached a year or more before, which wins the bet's fast side.
rows.who: the fast side of the growth bet

rows.line: Firms using AI grow larger and take decisions further from the people on the spot.
rows.settles: Firms getting smaller and more decentralised as they adopt AI.

rows.line: Work in the jobs most exposed to AI grows more intense before it grows shorter.
rows.settles: Paid hours in the most exposed work falling before output per worker rises.

rows.line: Labour's share of income falls as AI takes on more tasks, even as wages rise.
rows.settles: Labour's share holding while AI does a growing share of tasks.

rows.line: Care, teaching, hospitality and other work where the person is part of what is bought take a rising share of spending and jobs as AI spreads.
rows.settles: That work's share of spending and jobs falling as AI spreads.

rows.line: Publishers lose the visits that pay for what they produce.
rows.settles: Visits to publishers from search and AI answers rising.

folios.label: Value capture
folios.question: Where do the profits end up?

rows.line: Anthropic's revenue keeps growing about tenfold a year.
Money is not what is scarce.
Buyers sign up for AI capacity well ahead of using it, so Microsoft's contracted but undelivered business keeps growing faster than its revenue.
rows.settles: The backlog shrinking against revenue; it is one company's figure and counts contracts of every kind, much of it OpenAI's commitment to Microsoft's cloud.

rows.line: Companies selling AI products keep lower gross margins than classic software, because every use costs them the model's price.
rows.settles: AI product margins reaching those of classic software.

rows.line: Profit moves up to the labs
rows.settles: The chip makers' hold on the profit loosens if, over a year, the labs' share of the gross profit we can measure rises by five points while the chip makers' share falls by as much.

rows.line: The biggest cloud and platform companies spend more each year on buildings and equipment than AI earns in revenue.
rows.settles: AI's revenue overtaking that spending.

rows.line: NVIDIA and AMD take more than [test:chips_collect] of the gross profit they share with Microsoft's cloud arm and the estimates for OpenAI and Anthropic.
rows.settles: Their share falling below that line while chips stay short.

rows.line: Open models trail the best closed ones by less than [test:gap_stays_short], a shorter gap than this site calls normal.
rows.settles: The best closed models pulling away from open ones by that gap or more.

rows.line: Open models carry most of the tokens routed to OpenRouter's busiest models.
rows.settles: The closed models' share of those tokens climbing back as the gap to open models closes.

rows.line: Users keep most of the value
rows.settles: Users rather than sellers keep most of the value if what people say they would need to be paid to give AI up is more than double the revenue the leading labs and business buyers bring in.

rows.line: AI earns trillions of dollars a year in revenue before 2030.
AI needs about two trillion dollars of revenue a year by 2030 and falls short.
The gap between AI spending and the revenue to repay it keeps widening.
AI's revenue falls far short of what the spending on it needs to repay.
AI costs too much for the problems it can solve today.
The largest cloud companies spend many times more on AI buildings and chips than AI earns.
Apps that resell the labs' models see their margins shrink as their use grows.
rows.settles: A lab selling to apps below its public prices, or apps' margins holding as their use grows.

rows.line: NVIDIA's lead over other chip makers in sales for data centres keeps widening as AI spending grows.
rows.settles: Rival chip makers taking a growing share of data-centre chip sales while spending rises.

rows.line: The cloud companies start storing new chips instead of installing them, the sign Cahn watches for that data centres are running late [cite:cahn_2025].
rows.settles: New chips going into service as fast as they arrive.

rows.line: Much of AI's everyday work moves out of distant data centres onto people's own phones and laptops.
rows.settles: Everyday use staying in cloud data centres as capable open models get smaller.

rows.line: Only a handful of labs stay at the frontier, because it costs too much capital for more.
rows.settles: More than a handful of labs keeping pace with the best models.

rows.line: Being bought by a lab or a compute company becomes the usual way out for the start-ups that sell them data and tools.
rows.settles: The yearly count flattening, read only over quarters searched the same way. A later search that turns up deals missed earlier also raises the count, so it is not by itself a sign of more buying.

rows.line: The labs earn a growing share of their revenue from products and deployments inside their customers' firms rather than from selling access to their models by the token.
rows.settles: The labs' revenue staying mostly in selling access to their models by the token.

rows.line: Every firm ends up with a model of its own, trained on its own work.
rows.settles: Businesses' use of open models, the easiest kind to make one's own, falling further.

rows.line: Most businesses end up running models on machines they control rather than renting a lab's.
rows.settles: Businesses sticking with rented frontier models even as open models improve.

rows.line: Governments take direct stakes in the companies that make chips, power and models.
rows.settles: States staying lenders and buyers rather than owners.

rows.line: The people who use AI keep far more of its value than the firms that make it.
rows.settles: AI firms' profits growing as fast as the value their users get.

Can they keep learning without forgetting?

questions.note: No public test measures it yet.
questions.question: Can they tell cause from coincidence?
Can they carry a long project through on their own?

questions.note: HAL, a Princeton benchmark, scores how predictable agents' failures are; this site stores it but does not draw it yet.
questions.question: Do they know when they are unsure?
Is AI speeding up its own research?

questions.note: Whether data made by machines keeps its quality has no public test.
questions.question: Will data and computing run short?

questions.note: HAL also scores consistency, robustness and safety; only accuracy and overall reliability are drawn.
questions.question: Are they reliable enough for work where mistakes are costly?

questions.note: No public test verifies a model's goals.
questions.question: Can we verify what they are aiming at?
Do bigger models still surprise us?

words.label: Happening
words.meaning: Tonight's reading is what the prediction says.

words.label: Not happening
words.meaning: Tonight's reading is against it, or its own test fails.

words.label: Slower than said
words.meaning: Moving the way it says, but behind the timetable it gave.

words.label: Both sides expect this
words.meaning: The reading fits this prediction and its rival alike, so it settles nothing yet.

words.label: Too early to tell
words.meaning: No reading can test it yet, the reading is too old, or its date has not come.
